title: Social Engineering

objectives.text: Define social engineering, name the persuasion levers it relies on and put EC-Council's four attack phases in order
Tell phishing for information (T1598) from phishing for access (T1566) and place social engineering in MITRE ATT&CK
Recognize human-based techniques from a short scenario, including piggybacking vs tailgating, reverse social engineering and quid pro quo
Classify an insider threat (negligent, accidental, malicious, collusive, third-party, compromised) and name early warning signs
Explain how AI voice cloning and deepfake video change impersonation, and which process controls still stop it
Identify phishing variants (spear phishing, whaling, BEC, pharming, watering hole) and read the real domain behind a link
Describe impersonation on social networks and the main kinds of identity theft, and recognize SET, Gophish and Evilginx
Recognize smishing, quishing, malicious or repackaged apps, SIM swapping and MFA fatigue on mobile devices
Choose layered countermeasures: SPF, DKIM and DMARC, phishing-resistant MFA, callback verification, training, insider controls and identity theft response

readingMap.why: The persuasion levers and the four phases are asked directly; learn EC-Council's word lists.
Scenario questions hinge on one word (consent, who calls whom, what is offered); insider types and AI impersonation are here too.
Phishing variants, identity theft and phishing tools are the most tested part of the module.
Learn the names (smishing, quishing, repackaged apps, SIM swap); the mechanics repeat the computer-based ones.
Best-countermeasure questions are common; know SPF/DKIM/DMARC, phishing-resistant MFA and out-of-band verification.

labs.name: Analyze the headers of a suspicious email you received
labs.skill: Reading Received and Authentication-Results headers to judge SPF, DKIM and DMARC results and the real sending path

labs.name: Take the Google phishing quiz and write down the clue in each message
labs.skill: Spotting look-alike domains, mismatched links and pressure cues in realistic messages

labs.name: Run a phishing-awareness simulation against your own test mailbox with Gophish and MailHog
labs.skill: How simulation platforms track opens, clicks and reports, and how results feed an awareness program (own lab only, no real users)

labs.name: Phishing email analysis room on TryHackMe
labs.skill: Triage of phishing emails: sender, links, attachments and header analysis on a practice platform

feynmanPrompts: Explain to a new receptionist why a friendly, confident caller who knows the manager's name can still be an attacker, and what they should do before helping.
Walk through how a SIM swap lets an attacker reset a bank password, then explain why a FIDO2 security key would have stopped the takeover.
Explain what SPF, DKIM and DMARC each check, and why a business email compromise from a look-alike domain can pass all three.
